transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah. Um… I guess the short version is that I’m here because there’s been this situation with my ensemble, and it’s been going on long enough that I can’t just keep trying to explain it away.

I’m a composer and music director, and after this commission I did—almost two years ago now—things started feeling very coordinated, like a few people in the group were quietly trying to undermine the work. Not openly, not in a way where they’d say, “We don’t want this to succeed,” but through these little things: schedule changes that always seemed to disrupt the parts that mattered most, seating choices in rehearsal that affected how the piece came across, small comments that sounded casual but weren’t really casual if you knew the context.

And I know people will say, “Well, here’s the email,” or “Here are the rehearsal notes,” or “That seating was for balance,” and they’ve shown me things like that, but it doesn’t actually settle it for me. It feels like the explanations are there on paper, but underneath it there’s still this pattern. I’ve tried to let it go, honestly, but I can’t shake the certainty that something has been happening. That’s why I came in.
Can you tell me more about what you believe these people in your ensemble are trying to achieve by undermining your work?

I think… what they’re trying to do is make the work look weaker than it is without having to openly say they’re against it. Like, if they came out and said, “We don’t want this piece performed well,” that would be obvious and ugly and everyone would see it. But if it’s done through little adjustments—schedule changes that put the important rehearsals at bad times, seating choices that change how the sound comes across, these comments in rehearsal that seem harmless if you hear them once but start to add up—then they can sort of steer the whole thing downhill while still looking reasonable.

And I know that sounds hard to prove. That’s part of what’s so frustrating. Because when I ask about something, there’s always an explanation. There’s an email, or a note, or someone says it was for balance or logistics or availability. But I’ve been living with this pattern for almost two years now, since that commission, and it doesn’t feel random to me. It feels coordinated.

I think they want people to lose confidence in me, or to make the commission seem like it didn’t work, like maybe I wasn’t ready for it or the piece wasn’t strong enough. Not by saying that directly, but by making the rehearsals and performances just slightly off, again and again, so that the result reflects badly on me. I’ve tried to talk myself out of it, honestly, but I can’t shake the certainty that a few of them have been doing this quietly.
Have you ever experienced any sensations—like hearing voices, seeing things, or feeling something that others don’t seem to notice?

No, not really. I mean… I don’t think so. I’m not hearing voices or seeing things that other people don’t see, if that’s what you mean.

It’s more that I notice patterns in what people do and say—especially in rehearsals or emails—and other people will act like those things are just normal logistics or coincidences. But it’s not like a voice is telling me that, or I’m seeing something in the room that isn’t there. It’s more… the meaning of what’s happening feels very clear to me, even when other people say they don’t see it.

Even though others have provided explanations for the actions you're concerned about, do you still feel certain that these explanations are just cover-ups and that the real reason is a coordinated effort against your work?

Yes. I mean… yes, that’s the part I keep coming back to.

I understand that they have explanations. I’m not saying there’s literally no email or no practical reason written down somewhere. They’ll say, “This person wasn’t available,” or “We had to adjust the seating for balance,” or “That comment was just about the texture,” or whatever it is. And on the surface, each one can be made to sound reasonable. That’s almost what makes it harder, because if it were blatant, then at least I could point to it and say, “There, that’s what I mean.”

But for almost two years now, since that commission, I haven’t been able to shake the feeling—really more than a feeling, honestly—that a few people in the ensemble have been using those things as cover. The schedule changes, the seating choices, the little rehearsal comments that seem innocent unless you’ve been paying attention to the whole pattern… they all keep landing in a way that weakens the work or makes me look less prepared, less capable.

So when someone shows me notes or says it was just logistics, I hear that, but it doesn’t settle it. It feels like the official explanation is there, but the real reason is underneath it. And I know how that sounds. I do. But I’ve gone over it again and again, and I still feel certain this has been coordinated against my work.

Even though you’ve been given explanations for these actions and understand that others don’t see the same pattern, do you still believe, without any doubt, that this coordinated effort against your work is definitely happening?

Yes. I mean, that’s why I’m here, really. Because even when I try to be fair about it, even when I look at the emails or the notes or someone’s explanation of why a rehearsal time had to change or why the seating was adjusted, I still come back to the same conclusion.

It isn’t just one thing. If it were one schedule change, fine. If it were one strange comment in rehearsal, fine. But after the commission, it started feeling like these things kept happening in the same direction—always in ways that made the work harder to present well, or made me look like I hadn’t prepared properly, or made the piece seem weaker than it actually is.

And I know other people don’t see it the way I do. I know they say I’m reading too much into it, or that ensembles are messy and these things happen. But I’ve been sitting with this for almost two years, going over it again and again, and I can’t honestly say I have doubt about it. The explanations feel like explanations on paper, but not the real reason underneath. So yes, I do believe a few people have been quietly coordinating to undermine my work.
Have you ever confronted anyone or taken any action based on your belief that a few people in the ensemble have been coordinating against your work?

Yes… I mean, not in some dramatic way. I haven’t, like, stormed into a rehearsal and accused everyone or sent some huge email saying I know what they’re doing. I’ve been careful about that, partly because I know how it would sound, and partly because professionally that could backfire badly.

What I have done is ask for more clarification than I probably used to. If a rehearsal plan changes, or if there’s a seating decision, or if someone phrases something in an email in a way that feels pointed, I’ll reread it several times and sometimes write back asking what exactly was meant, or whether there was another reason behind the decision. I try to keep it polite and practical, but honestly it takes a lot more energy than it should.

Rehearsals are harder too, not because I can’t do them, but because I’m watching things more closely. I’ll be thinking, “Why did they say it that way?” or “Why is that person being placed there?” and then I still have to keep working, conducting or discussing the music or whatever the situation is. So it adds this whole extra layer.

But I haven’t lost any work over it. I’m still functioning. I’m still doing the professional things I need to do, answering emails, preparing scores, showing up, taking care of myself. It’s more that everything around rehearsals and communication has become heavier. I spend more time checking, rereading, asking follow-up questions, trying to make sure I’m not missing what’s really going on.
Can you tell me if you've had any thoughts or beliefs that others might consider strange or untrue, but you feel certain are real, even when no one else agrees with you?

Yes. I mean… I suppose that’s exactly what this is, isn’t it? I know other people would probably say it sounds unlikely, or that I’m connecting things that don’t belong together, but to me it feels real. More than feels real, honestly.

For almost two years, since that commission, I haven’t been able to shake the certainty that a few people in the ensemble started quietly working against me. Not openly, not in a way where they’d say something obvious, but through things that can be explained away if you look at each one separately. Schedule changes. Seating choices. Little comments in rehearsals that seem harmless on paper but land in a very particular way. Things that make my work harder to present well or make me look less prepared.

And yes, they’ve shown me emails or notes or given explanations that are supposed to account for it. I understand those explanations exist. But they don’t convince me. They feel like the surface version, the acceptable version, while the real reason is underneath it. I know that if I described it to someone who wasn’t there, they might think I’m being unreasonable. But I’ve gone over the pattern so many times that I can’t really see it as coincidence anymore.
Have you had any other beliefs or suspicions, outside of this situation with the ensemble, that others might not share or find believable, but you feel certain are true?

No, not really. At least, nothing like this.

I’ve tried to think about that, because I know if I say I’m certain about one thing, the next obvious question is whether I’m seeing patterns everywhere. But I don’t think I am. I don’t walk around thinking strangers are involved, or that unrelated people are sending me messages, or anything like that. It’s really centered on this ensemble and what happened around the commission and the people connected to that.

I mean, I can be cautious in professional settings now, maybe more than I used to be, because once something like this happens you start paying closer attention to tone and decisions and who says what. But I wouldn’t say I have other fixed suspicions outside of that. My concern is pretty specific. It’s this situation.
Have you ever had any beliefs or suspicions that aren’t related to this situation with the ensemble, which others might not share or find believable, but you feel certain are true?

No… I don’t think so. Not outside of the ensemble situation.

I mean, the reason I’m here is really because of that one thing: after the commission, I became convinced — and I still am convinced — that a few people in the ensemble started doing things quietly to undermine my work. Not in some obvious, cartoonish way, but through things like schedule changes, seating choices, and these small comments in rehearsals that seem casual if you’re not paying attention, but when you’re actually there and you see the pattern, they don’t feel casual.

And I know people have tried to explain it away. They’ll show me emails, or notes, or say, “No, this was just because of availability,” or “That seating choice was for balance,” things like that. I hear the explanations. I understand what they’re saying. I just don’t believe that’s the real reason underneath it.

But outside of that? No, I’m not walking around with other suspicions about unrelated people or other situations. It’s this. It’s been almost two years of not being able to shake this certainty about what happened after the commission.
